A liquid containing rotating fixed vortices at an integer spacing showing the a) Nernst effect, where a magnetic field emerges due to the flow perpendicular to the vortices, as well as the appearance of a viscosity that resists both the vortices and a flow along their lines, and c) the Vortex Line Entropy Law, which states that the density of Vortex Line Entropy is the same as the density of Vortex Line Residual Resistance. These findings are consistent with a form of Ohm's Law that takes into account the vortices in the Lorentz force, and they apply to various types of fluids, including liquid helium and liquid crystals.

Advanced prediction and control systems have been developed and refined, but they often suffer from limited effectiveness. This is because their design is heavily influenced by the accuracy of the underlying model, which can be flawed. This issue is exasperated in complex and changing environments. To overcomes this shortcoming, this paper presents a novel approach of introducing flexibility into the prediction control systems by incorporating learning algorithms that can adapt to environment changes. In particular, we propose an iterative method of combining nonlinear predictive control with on-line adaptive regression techniques to gradually enhance the performance of the control system and adapt to the environment. This paper demonstrates the proposed approach on the challenging task of underwater vehicle performance optimization and trajectory tracking in the simulated marine environment.

Using deep learning for stock valuation and time series prediction has been the subject of various research studies, with some even combining multiple neural networks to improve results, although there's still room for enhancement. In this work, we propose a novel approach that incorporates several state-of-the-art techniques, including BERT and GAN, to develop an efficient stock valuation model, with a particular focus on generating realistic numerical data from historical stock prices. The results indicate that our method outperforms a range of baseline models and, in particular, beats a widely used industry-based forecasting model, with our system also demonstrating higher profitability on automated trading, with an optimal risk-adjusted return, for stock investments. The code is made available on the accompanying GitHub repository, with figures illustrated using a range of statistical tools, including heat maps, bar charts, line graphs, and pie charts.

This work introduces a novel shared memory formalism called SCATTER, which utilizes a shared envelope concept. We outline its basics in this work and demonstrate the effectiveness of SCATTER by providing an abstraction theorem in this inductive framework. Furthermore, this paper outlines key features of the verification tool GSSC, which leverages the capabilities of the Coq proof assistant to facilitate proofs within the SCATTER framework.

This research delves into the production of two Higgs bosons at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with elevated energies, specifically 3 TeV and up to 1.5-2.5 TeV. The study primarily concentrates on a scenario where two Higgs bosons are produced through the di-Higgs effective field theory (EFT), highlighting the C^6 driven process that involves bottom-quark annihilation. Because the relevant process for the EFT-driven production of two Higgs bosons, namely top-querk fusion, has a negligible impact compared to the existing constraints, we can anticipate a substantial potential for research, which ranges from 5.5 to more than 25 times greater than the sensitivities that can be achieved with the Current Large Hadron Collider. In order to estimate the potential for research, we consider both experimental uncertainties that are well-understood and those that are less clear, which pertain to the Higgs boson branching ratios and detection efficiencies. The study also discusses the implications of these potentials for research, which could shed light on the nature of the Higgs boson and explain why there are not more than four generations of quarks and leptons.

We derive the Euler-Peres equations from the generalised geodatic variational principle using the appropriate generalisation of the geodatic action. Based on this result, we develop the appropriate Lagrangians for the Einstein-Gromer-Laubin theory.

A connection between holographic field theories and five-dimensional gravitational theories corresponds, under the AdCFT conjecture, to a highly accurate approximation. Our research focuses on four-field theories with an $\mathcal{N}=4$ conformal symmetry and an $SU(N)$ symmetry that interact with a constant negative scalar field. We investigate the behavior of two well-separated, parallel shock waves in this series of interacting systems by utilizing holographic technology. These shock waves are linked to localized, highly energetic regions of the field theory that are isolated from one another due to the Cauchy surface separation. Through the application of a series of calculations based on gravitational actions, we determine the correlation between these two field theories at the next order of an $\epsilon^4$ expansion, which represents a technical challenge due to the presence of subleading terms derived from an optimal geometric series. Our results are supported by a new geometric principle that relates optimal surfaces to minimal surfaces in five-dimensional space and to a geometric series of optimal surfaces.

We calculated the drag experienced by a cylindrical material as it moves through a bed of granular particles saturated with fluid. Assuming the cylinder has an anisotropic shape and moves in any direction, we used Darcy's law and force balance principles to develop a model for drag. This model considers the permeability of both the granular bed and the cylinder itself, as well as its shape and direction of movement. We expressed the drag as a quadratic form based on these factors and investigated the resulting effects, including how the cylinder's shape and direction of movement influence the drag experienced. Furthermore, we explored how these factors contribute to the entrainment of the cylinder. Furthermore, we demonstrated that our model can accurately describe the behavior of cylindrical materials moving through beds of particles, regardless of their shape.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a gas-rich galaxy with a history of star formation outbursts and associated large-scale outflows. Our data showed that large outflows are triggered when a galaxy's star formation rate surpasses the Eddington limit, a phenomenon caused by processes such as stellar mass loss and the collapse of giant molecular clouds. The key feature of this galaxy, named UGc98-14, is its massive outflows that extend for a quarter of its visible length and spread across the inner regions with an angular width of a tenth. The spatial distribution of these outflows provides a crucial insight into the role of feedback mechanisms in galaxy evolution. A new model, called DISCO, taking into account the rotating and unstable nature of galaxy disks, reveals that the combination of outflows and star formation interacting within such disks often leads to a self-regulating process that controls future star formation and contributes to the evolution of galaxies.

A significant challenge in our modern world is achieving energy efficiency in numerous systems. Accelerating progress toward this goal requires numerous expensive experiments. Due to the high cost, a traditional experimental approach becomes impractical for determining optimal settings in complex systems with numerous parameters. In order to reduce the number of required experiments, we propose a novel organized optimization framework called BoGraph. This framework efficiently identifies optimal settings in systems with many parameters by quickly navigating vast settings spaces and remembering the outcomes of past trials. A data-driven method, Organize Learning, is incorporated into BoGraph to utilize information from previous trials and streamline the search for optimal configurations. Organize Learning is based on a multilayer perceptron neural network, which leverages historical data to accelerate the optimization process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of BoGraph through its application to tuning the energy efficiency of a complex scientific simulation.

Our research examined triangular flow using three different matchable observables, data from the STAR detector at RHIC for 200 GeV Au+Au collisions with three rapidity centrality selections have been compared to model results. Results from Cu+Cu and Au+Au collisions at 20 GeV RHIC were also considered, and results from the PHENIX detector with three different centrality selections were compared to model results for both energies and for 62 GeV NHIC with a Cu+Al beam with two different velocities were considered as well. First, we demonstrated that initial energy density can be extracted from initial geometry using energy density and entropy results from transport models and from an initial energy density using final particle density, this method was then utilized to determine the initial energy density of 200 GeV Au+Au and 20 GeV Au+Au collisions, 20 GeV Au+Al and Cu+Al and 62 GeV NHIC collisions. Next, we demonstrated that initial entropy density can be derived from initial geometry using the entropy of the final particle density for both 200 GeV and 20 GeV collisions, this was then compared to an initial entropy derived from the initial energy density and the temperature of the energy density. Finally, we found that flow coefficient d$v_3$/dy can be predicted from initial elliptic and triangular density using final particle density, this was then compared to an estimate of d$v

The rapid expansion of the Web 3.0 ecosystem has resulted in a surge of Web resources with limited interoperability and trustworthiny, thus prompting the creation of Web 3+.  One approach to improving data interoperability and reliability on the World Wide Web is implementing data validation mechanisms, often referred to as "quality gates," before incorporating data into larger projects such as Linked Open Data (LOD).  However, existing data quality tools are inefficient due to their pairwise comparison methods, leading to poor scalability as datasets grow in size.  To address this limitation, a novel graph-structured data evaluation method is introduced, allowing for the rapid assessment of large-quality datasets by isolating low-quality "faulty triangles" within a tripartite graph format.  Through empirical testing, the proposed method shows up to a 100-fold improvement in evaluation efficiency compared to traditional approaches.

The method of identifying model parameters from observed data is called offline parameter estimation and is utilized in various contexts, from modeling dynamic systems monitored at discrete intervals to modeling processes with posthumous analysis. Due to the intricate nature of dynamic systems and the unavailability of reverse control, the method is still extensively used. The author's earlier work introduced a new framework for offline parameter estimation based on maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), utilizing a conditional likelihood function and a Monte Carlo approximation to address infeasible calculations. A significant advantage of this approach is the ability to estimate parameters for a conditional likelihood function that cannot be calculated directly, along with a new method avoiding the computation of future states given current conditions. The author demonstrates the effectiveness of this method through results from detailed simulations and real-world data, showing that their approach outperforms other prominent techniques in terms of accuracy, especially in data with noise. Additionally, the author introduces a new algorithm that combines a profiled likelihood function and iterative reweighted least squares, and conducts a comprehensive comparative study. The author's approach is shown to often compete favorably with the benchmark methods, consistently ranking in the top two and consistently displaying lower error mean standard deviations.

This paper is part of a series investigating chemical compositions in Seyfert galaxies using the SHINES integral field spectrograph, which obtained high-resolution spectra for four low-ionization Seyferts and two active galactic nuclei. Researchers found significant electron densities in a subset of nuclei, but the main focus was on examining [N III] $\lambda\lambda$990, 995 emission outside the standard Agn projection. They discovered unusual "surprises" in two galaxies where a high-electron density was detected in low-ionization regions, alongside areas of low electron density with "soft" spectra. Further analysis of "surprises" revealed distinct spectral characteristics, with high-density regions exhibiting harder spectra and high velocities seen in [N III] $\lambda$995 emission indicating possible jet activity. These findings led to more in-depth exploration of complex interactions between active galactic nuclei and their surrounding environments, which could be fueled by efficient cooling processes or jet interaction.

As applications move to less capable devices and less reliable devices, ensuring they adapt to limited resources and unreliable infrastructure becomes crucial for optimal performance in energy-efficient and cost-effective environments. Our proposed framework enables automated assessment of applications' adaptability by generating optimal configuration options and identifying suitable combinations of settings to ensure edge deployments meet performance goals. By leveraging advanced solvers, we can efficiently explore a vast configuration space, potentially including millions of options, to find the ideal setting combinations for improved edge app performance and reduced operational costs. An automatically created configuration model streamlines this process, reducing complex optimization problems to more manageable forms, as demonstrated in our evaluations of real-world applications under varied edge conditions.

The ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has extensively analyzed rare beauty meson decay events and measures angle differences in neutral B meson decays that violate CP symmetry, with an anomaly of 3.3 sigma for certain decay reactions. Data collected by the ATLAS detector include 20 million beauty meson decay events and 0.6 attobecquerels of proton collision data from 2015 at the LHC. Here we detail studies concerning beauty meson decays involving an imbalance of matter and antimatter, and an uncommon process in which two photons are emitted from a neutral beauty meson.

The current traffic simulation tools utilized in the validation of autonomous driving technologies typically generate fake scenes through manipulation, which often results in unrealistic driver behavior. Machine learning-based approaches, in particular, require extensive high-quality annotated data for high-performance models, which are frequently compromised by artificial traffic conditions, undermining their value. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel data collection methodology called SceneGen, which involves modifying real driving conditions to the point where even human drivers struggle to navigate them safely. This enables us to gather high-quality annotated data with reliable labels, leveraging the capabilities of sensor suites typically employed in autonomous driving vehicles. SceneGen is versatile and can be applied to various road types, from highways to urban streets. Furthermore, it serves as a general method for generating high-quality annotated data in the creation of real-world driving scenarios.

On a Cayley tree, we prove the existence of new, moderate cyclicity measures for the Ising model, occurring when the interaction strength oscillates between two values at adjacent bonds. For these measures, we identify the potential density function and demonstrate that existing measure exclusivity applies, meaning they cannot coexist with strictly periodic measures that exhibit cycles of any length other than two.

The choice of discretization method and numerical solution technique should ideally be independent, as each has distinct advantages and drawbacks. Our research focuses on the potential of preconditioned Krylov methods when applied to discretized problems that maintain key physical properties, such as their semi-discrete formulations. While many monotone, convex-based schemes come with inherent drawbacks, their transformation into structure-preserving formats yields valuable properties, notably enhanced preconditionability. Specifically, we demonstrate that certain schemes, although not preserving positivity on their own, can solve relevant problems effectively, as their exponential growth rates are limited by their continuous counterparts, and can be further optimized through suitable preconditioning. Our analysis reveals that an alternating direction implicit (ADI) scheme can achieve the same result and is comparable to established methods, such as ZZET, in terms of solution accuracy and efficiency.

We investigated the formation of dust in supernova 1987A's surroundings and found that its low metallicity makes dust formation challenging. Using a 1D model, we analyzed a range of conditions similar to those in which 1987A occurred, considering different timescales, shock velocities, and progenitor masses. Our analysis revealed that while some metal species like silicon could create small dust particles, they would eventually be destroyed. Only chromium was able to form stable, growing dust particles. The key to understanding this lies in the rates at which metals are deposited and destroyed, which are influenced by the shock velocity and metallicity but balanced in the case of chromium. The outcome also depended on whether 19877A's surroundings contained sufficient cyanide to initiate a reverse shock. If present, the shock would be slowed, enhancing the chances for dust growth. However, given the lack of chromium metallicity in 1987A's surroundings, any dust that did form would be rare and difficult to detect. We speculate that future observations of similar supernovae with higher chromium metallicity could provide valuable insights into these phenomena.

Detection systems in distant areas, often referred to as distant detection, are crucial for a comprehensive and wide-ranging perception system in the automotive sector. Currently, most detection algorithms demonstrate outstanding performance in short and intermediate distances. Nonetheless, their effectiveness significantly declines in distant scenarios due to object shrinkage, masked visibility, and critical scenarios. To tackle these challenges, the Far3Det framework is introduced. The primary components of Far3Det include the Feature Fusion Module, the Scene-Aware Masked Sampling Strategy, and the Far3D Detection Module, each addressing the challenges of small, mask-aware objects. The Scene-Aware Masked Sampling Strategy enhances the detection module's capability to handle objects that are both small and partially obscured, whereas the Far3D Detection Module employs a hybrid approach combining set-based and point-based methods to effectively deal with masked objects that lack complete 3D parameter estimation. The results of the Far3Det module demonstrate superior performance, particularly in distant scenarios, when compared to existing methods on the nuScenes dataset. The integration of the Feature Fusion Module, Scene-Aware Masked Sampling Strategy, and the Far3D Detection Module leads to notable enhancements in distant 3D detection performance. The proposed methods also yield significant improvements, amounting to a 11.8% increase in Average Orientation Parameter error for objects located more than 18 meters away from the sensor.

The primary goal of this study is to present the foundational concepts of a quantum machine learning algorithm, specifically designed to efficiently find ground states of molecules as a series of data points. Current methods, although effective, can be complicated by the need to represent Hamiltonians using matrices, a process that can be computationally expensive. In contrast, our approach eschews this requirement, instead focusing on identifying pattern within data sets that characterize ground states. Given its relative simplicity, this method has the potential to be easily adapted to quantum computers, with an application demonstrated in finding the electronic ground state of a hydrogen molecule.

Converting a 3D object's representation from volume to surface format is a crucial step in various applied fields such as computer animation, computer vision, and medical diagnosis. Traditional methods align the two representations rigidly, however, humans and animals often change their shapes flexibly without affecting their overall volume. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel, flexible volume-to-surface alignment technique using a data-driven biomechanical model. This method modifies the mechanical properties of a 3D object's representation, including its density and elasticity, to match the external shape format. We tested the technique on synthetic deformable objects and medical MRI scans of kidneys, successfully achieving accurate and efficient results.

For a stationary, spherically symmetric universe described by a metric, we're looking for transformations that preserve its underlying structure, specifically those related to its energy and momentum. We're looking for a set of equations to identify the characteristics of these transformation agents, or symmetry generators, when they are related to the universe's fundamental laws. We also provide examples of universe scenarios where these transformations play a key role, including one that satisfies a long-standing conjecture.

In self-supervised scene flow estimation, most approaches utilize paired videos and corresponding optical flow maps to train valid models, however, they are vulnerable to corrupted training data from incorrect predictions and the inclusion of outlier points. To enhance the robustness of this process, traditional metric learning methods rely on weighted losses that calculate explicit distances between valid and incorrect samples, consequently exposing the encoder to deceptive and distorted metric information provided by flawed incorrect samples. In this research, we introduce a novel strategy that utilizes the implicit distances between three types of samples (outlier, incorrect, and valid) by learning an implicit metric space that separates only valid samples from the mixture of incorrect and outlier samples. We also introduce two innovative modules, a confidence-aware boundary refinement module and an adaptive pairwise weighting module, to (i) identify and correct boundary-related incorrect samples and (ii) identify adversarial incorrect samples and discarding them from incorrect samples. Extensive experiments on the KITTI and Sintel datasets show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art self-supervised flow estimation methods on both monocular and dual settings.

In the realm of hardware-efficient AI, we have made significant half-width advances in Static Neural Networks (SNNs). Now, the focus has shifted towards Random Neural Networks (RNNs), which offer comparable accuracy but potentially greater energy efficiency due to their binary-weight and binary-output design. However, optimizing both the network architecture and the sampling-based training process has proven challenging. To address this, we have designed an energy-aware Random Neural Network (eRNN) that leverages a diverse set of layer types and enables the neural units to collaborate in decoding complex data patterns. The eRNN's innovative Design Space Exploration (DSE) algorithm dynamically adjusts the network's structure and refines its classification performance. When tested on several hardware platforms, our eRNN consistently outperformed both traditional and customized SNNs and RNNs across multiple classification tasks, demonstrating substantial reductions in energy consumption while maintaining competitive accuracy levels.

We investigate the thermodynamic characteristics of a spin-aligned strange quark star, taking into account interactions quarks experience in a finite temperature and external magnetic field. Using a van der Waals equation modified for spin alignment, we derive the temperature and magnetic field conditions under which the strange quark star can maintain stability. Furthermore, we analyze how these factors influence the temperature profile and overall size of the strange quark star.

A recently introduced concept of an ideal matching in a graph $G$, a matching that contains a specific subgraph $H$ as a component, was first introduced by Goto in 2009. In 2014, Hegde and Shadrang extended the notion of an ideal matching and began exploring its properties. This paper proves that a 3-edge-colored cubic graph with an ideal matching as a $K_{2,4}$ component always has a Hamiltonian circuit, and provides a counterexample to Hegde and Shadrang's conjecture, showing the colorability of ideal matchings in cubic graphs is not always 3-edge.

Let $A$ consist of $n$ distinct polynomials, each with coefficients in a ring $R$ and degrees no higher than $d$. If $n$ exceeds $d$ and $n$ is a positive integer, then $A$ can be expanded into 'blocks' $B$ with the property that for any combination of elements from $B$, the sum cannot be factored. We prove that for any $n$ that is not 3, then $A$ can have at most $n$ blocks, and if $n$ is 3, the maximum number of blocks $q$ varies based on $d$ and the nature of the ring $R$, specifically, it is infinite if $R$ is a field of a characteristic that is a prime other than 2 or 3 and a characteristic that is greater than $d$, but it is finite if $R$ is a field of a characteristic 2 or 3 and a characteristic that is less than or equal to $d$, in which case it is denoted as $M(d, R)$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for any $d$, there exist rings $R_1$ and $R_2$ and arrangements $B_1$ and $B_2$ such that they each cannot be factored and they each have $d+3$ and $2d+4$ elements respectively, in which case it is proven that $M(d, R)$

The proper use of system calls by a software application significantly affects its performance and resource consumption. Unfortunately, optimizing system call patterns is usually affected by performance local minima and requires extensive tuning. To address this issue, we introduce Timeloops, a performance-tuning framework that automatically discovers system call policies to enhance performance. Timeloops employs machine learning algorithms to create system call patterns, which are then used as input to a closed performance loop to evaluate their effectiveness. The framework leverages containerized microservices for efficient testing and comparison of different system call patterns. As a result, Timeloops is capable of outperforming manual tuning, as well as various performance optimization techniques, in a range of benchmark scenarios, often achieving similar or better performance without the need for performance modeling.

Investigating the possibility of a Pseudo-Goldstone Dark Matter (PGDM) within the Standard Model Extension comprises a novel approach, yet there has been insufficient exploration in this area. In this paper, we introduce the concept of PGM as the dark sector's pseudo-Nambu Goldstone boson, arising from a broken $B-L$ symmetry within the Standard Model Extension. By incorporating this framework and introducing dark quarks with non-zero $B-L$ charges, we can expand upon the Minimal $B-L$ Extension of the Standard Model. Introducing two Higgs triplets enables a dark sector Higgs mechanism that generates mass for the Dark Perioh ($D$). The decay of a heavy neutral Higgs into a pair of $D$ anti-$D$ provides the necessary conditions for the thermal production of dark matter. Our analysis indicates that the Dark Perioh meets the observed dark matter abundance thresholds through this thermal production mechanism, with distinct implications for direct detection experiments depending on the nature of the Dark Perioh's mass spectrum.

A variation of the probability hypothesis density filter has been developed to account for new targets appearing on a regular grid, applicable in scenarios like target tracking using global positioning systems and remote sensing, where sensors cover a defined area. This approach can also serve as a testbed for theoretical concepts of the global movement hypothesis in PMBM filtering. By using place representations for targets within a continuous space, the proposed method reduces the computational demands while maintaining filtering capabilities. Proof of the closure property and the updated recursion equations for this approach are provided, along with a comparison to the PMBMGaussianECS filter. However, there are challenges with implementing this approach due to the potential for performance degradation when targets appear outside the grid boundaries, although an update rule can be established to overcome this issue.

This study examines the null controllability of a community dynamics system in two dimensions.
The system's complexity is reduced to a singular equation involving the Laplace operator, with the equation degenerately behaving at a specific point in the domain.
As a direct consequence of our main finding, we also establish the null controllability of an elliptic-degenerate heat equation at a given time, with the equation degenerately occurring either at an interior point of the domain or at its boundary.

In soccer, making the right decisions can significantly influence the outcome of a match, but there's still much unknown about how decisions interact in various situations, especially during crucial moments. This research employs advanced methods to analyze decisions during matches and utilizes a reinforcement learning approach to evaluate the effectiveness of those decisions based on team performance. By assessing the advantages of taking alternative actions, a reinforcement learning model trained on data can provide enhanced near-optimal solutions. A neural network is then trained with help from this model, allowing it to faster make optimal moves while also benefiting from the enhanced near-optimal strategy in situations where making the best choice takes a long time. Experimental results indicate that these strategies outperform a standard approach in evaluating soccer matches' scores. Moreover, simulations suggest that taking risks can be a valuable approach in certain scenarios, such as set pieces, and that the value of these risks varies depending on the situation.

In seismic data processing, waveform inversion is an advanced technique used to improve the accuracy of geological models by analyzing the timing and strength of recorded signals. A significant challenge in this process is determining the absolute phase of the simulated signals, which can be effectively addressed through the incorporation of frequency shifts into the objective function. However, directly utilizing relative phase information requires solving a non-differentiable problem, thus necessitating the development of novel algorithms capable of leveraging phase information for more effective seismic inversion. In this research, we propose introducing the concept of inversion using relative phase information and demonstrate how this approach can be applied to interpret signals in the time domain after amplification, which is shown to yield more stable and efficient results with fewer parameters than their frequency-domain counterparts. Our findings also indicate that a novel implementation of the adjoint method can efficiently calculate the required gradients required for optimization, which are otherwise computationally expensive to obtain through conventional methods. A synthetic test is conducted to verify the effectiveness of the proposed approach, which is also found to be successfully integrated into an iterative optimization framework combining the adjoint method and the L-BFGS algorithm for more refined results.

The nonreversibility of optical compression using polymers remains a distinctive feature exploited in optical components like isolators and circulators.  Although traditional designs achieve high performance, they rely on bulky devices.  We have developed a new class of irreversible compressors through quantum-induced nonreciprocity using an ultrathin, magnetized 2D material and have validated their exceptional compression performance in simulations and experiments.  Our novel approach has an ultra-high compression ratio of up to 10^8 at 1550 nm and extremely low insertion loss.  At a specific power level, our compressor exhibits a superior performance improvement by many orders of magnitude compared to polymer-based alternatives.  Notably, our model has a distinct advantage of power scalability, and as such, achieves an improved compression ratio by several orders of magnitude in our experiment by 10^4.  As a result, we have discovered that magnetooptics-based devices may offer a highly efficient and compact solution for future photonic applications.

We analyzed the 2019 X-ray emission from low-hard X-ray bands of X-ray emission lines and a quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) in low frequencies from the X-ray binary IGR J19294+1816.  At the peak of the 2019 outburst, this source exhibited a narrow, narrow line centered at 27.5 keV, likely a cyclotron feature, and an low-frequency QPO at 0.17 Hz with a significant semi-width.  By comparing these observations to data from 2018, we found a difference in the line's intensity but a consistent cyclotron frequency.  We also observed that the line's width and the QPO's frequency remained largely unchanged.  These findings indicate that the neutron star's surface area, the accretion flux, and spin frequency did not substantially change, with the variation in disk inner edge angle accounting for most of the 2018-2019 outburst difference.  Additionally, we compared these observations to a 1999 episode of the same source, discovering that the line's parameters and the QPO's frequency were essentially the same, further confirming that IGR J19294+1816 has experienced multiple low-hard X-ray flares throughout its history. In a chaotic environment, the dynamics of a lattice-based, noise-influenced Ising model lead to an unexpected opportunity for two species to coexist through a competition-colonization balance, without the need for one species to dominate another. The tradeoff between the paramagnetic phase associated with species A's territorial stability and the disordered phase of species B's ability to inhabit any lattice site, enables their equilibrium habitation of the environment. The boundary between these regions dictates the species distribution, with finer features influencing colonization capabilities. However, the added complexity of species interaction within this model provides an unexpected indication of dual species survival under circumstances where only the disordered phase is accessible, as demonstrated in simulations of a turbulent environment.

Analog timekeeping instruments called sundials depend on the presence of sunlight to function, recording the passage of time through the shadows they cast. As an exercise in scientific education and preservation, this project aims to create a comprehensive database of Indonesian sundials by gathering their characteristics, geographical location, and design specifics via a simple web interface. The system utilizes geospatial mapping, open data principles, and web technologies like HTML5, jQuery, and REST APIs to facilitate seamless collaboration and future data integration.

This research focuses on a novel wireless technology where the Intellect Reflecting Surface (IRS) is integrated with an wireless power transfer system. A multi-user D2D communication scenario is also considered, in which an information and energy transfer pair use their connected IRS node to help a power-hungry D2D pair, enabling an efficient coexistence of D2D communications. A total maximization problem is formulated to maximize the total data rate and minimize power consumption simultaneously, subject to a power consumption constraint. A corresponding coexistence optimization problem is developed and an optimal solution is provided for it. A semi-greedy algorithm is proposed for the original optimization problem, along with a theoretical analysis of its performance. A conversion rule is developed to convert the solution of the coexistence problem to that of the total maximization problem. A case study is provided to validate the advantages of different optimization strategies, as well as key factors that influence system data rates and power consumption. Further analysis of these factors is provided to offer more design insights for system parameters.

This paper outlines the development of a control system for an electro-optical distance measurement setup, specifically one that utilizes an LDV system to obtain two-dimensional data. The goal is to collect a large number of distance measurements in a short amount of time, with data points linked to their corresponding x, y coordinates. To achieve this, we have employed a LDV system based on the LDV-Delta-D method, which involves rapidly varying the frequency of the laser source to differentiate between small time delays and small distance changes. The system's performance depends on the rate at which the electronic switch can toggle between make and break contacts. By utilizing a microcontroller to control a computerized switching system, we were able to achieve a switching rate of up to 10 kHz, which yielded a maximum measurable distance of around 2 cm with a time period of 0.1 seconds. In order to prevent the system from becoming overloaded with data, we have implemented a method for filtering out unnecessary data, with a success rate of around 85%. The entire process takes approximately 1.5 seconds to complete, with the entire electronic system operating at a power level of around 12 volts and 2 amps.

The use of high-level deformations of the electrostatic phase disc in the TEM allows for the correction of distortions, such as those caused by the objective lens aberration, in a versatile and customizable way. Our research indicates that a programmable phase disc can effectively compensate for the non-ideality of the objective lens in the TEM, yielding a corrected imaging result that surpasses the depth of field range. Moreover, the compensation range of the programmable phase disc can be extended to a significant proportion, approximately 85%, of the non-ideality objective lens' transfer function support range, y = 1/λC_{disc}. The design of the programmable phase disc serves a dual purpose, facilitating both the TEM's imaging corrector and the creation of a unique type of optical corrector for the disc's equivalent circumference C_{disc}.

The success of generative conversation models relies on their ability to effectively communicate key topics, much like how meaningful encoder representations are crucial for subsequent applications. Our research aims to evaluate the encoder of a generative conversation model in detail. We propose a conversation task as a way to assess the encoder and propose three novel tasks based on key communication principles. Our experiments reveal that the model's randomly initialized conversations perform well in our proposed tasks, but fall short of human levels. As the conversation length increases, the model's performance generally improves. Interestingly, the task of summarizing the conversation proves to be the easiest, while following the conversation requires significantly more data. Our findings also suggest that explicit control mechanisms, like those seen in following a particular style, are more feasible than those relying on implicit assumptions, like following the leading tone. Moreover, we observe that the conversation model's encoder behaves similarly to that of a cloner, but with a key distinction: it generates representations that are easier to decode but not as controllable.

Building automated facilities for urban search and rescue operations requires a robust system to identify people in need. This study presents a novel approach to detecting humans, vehicles, and various objects using LiDAR data from multiple angles, based on deep learning techniques. By combining single-angle detectors with directional attention mechanisms and by training a shared encoder for feature extraction, our proposed method, AttDLNet, efficiently uses fewer resources while maintaining high accuracy. Tests on the MSDL dataset demonstrate superior performance of AttDLNet compared to alternatives, with precise results in search and rescue scenarios requiring the identification of individuals, vehicles, and other objects.

Today, video consumes a vast majority of all internet traffic andTV quality videos are increasingly popular on the web.  However, web encoding standards don't always match user device encoding capabilities, which can cause compatibility issues, underscoring the need for video transcoding.  This study investigates how video transcoding can effectively be performed on a cloud environment with diverse types of computers, taking into account user requirements and available resources.  A new algorithm is developed to transcode videos efficiently by allocating resources based on the complexity of the video, which is then simulated using an Apache CloudStack cloud environment, and found to reduce transcoding time and costs by up to 22% and 18% respectively compared to existing methods.

This paper explores the impact of exchange and correlation on the quantum Hall effect in doped graphene, considering both semi-local Lichtenstein-Kalm\'ar-Wheeler (LKW) forces and local Hubbard forces in a quantum Hall regime. Our mean-field analysis reveals a quantum Hall ferromagnet with shielding of in-plane interactions due to H\'enney-Monkhorst forces, and demonstrates that the LKW force plays a more significant role in quantum Hall systems compared to normal systems. Specifically, we found that at high temperatures, the quantum Hall ferromagnetism undergoes checking, with the H\'enney-Monkhorst force being insufficient to compensate for thermal disruption, even when the system is in a quantum Hall normal state. Specifically, we discovered an important role of the semi-local LKW interaction in quantum Hall systems, with an order of magnitude longer range than in normal systems. Specifically, we found an interesting competition between thermal shielding and phase transitions, with an order of magnitude difference between the thermal shielding and the local Hubbard interaction. This an order of magnitude difference between thermal shielding and the local interaction may be an experimental signature of thermal shielding. Continuous improvements in speech synthesis systems have made them近乎 indistinguishable from real human voices, yet they often overlook the significance of context in spoken language. Research has shown that written text alone is usually insufficient for teaching language models how to grasp the full nuance of linguistic meaning. Building upon this, we propose a novel approach that incorporates context into speech synthesis by utilizing a masking technique, which allows the model to focus on the most critical information necessary to convey a message's true meaning. We have developed the MaskedDialogue dataset, which includes a vast collection of multi-turn conversations spanning 13,000+ discussions and over 50,000 individual utterances, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our context-aware synthesis model through a series of comparative analyses using this dataset.

We examine the stability of the trivial solution for a specific setup involving the Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator, where the equation's parameters lead to a discrete spectrum for the Klein-Gordon part. This study also explores how the Klein-Gordon component's spectrum affects the stability of the system. This work is part of a broader investigation into splitting Hamiltonian systems and how their components influence the stability of trivial solutions, as highlighted in related papers.

Q-ball studies in a dark sector have a rich variety, and we examine Q-balls in detail, covering their general properties and specific scenarios. Our analysis considers the standard, hollow, and multi-core Q-balls, with the latter two being less understood. Utilizing an effective field theory, we derive the parameters of Q-balls in models featuring quadratic, quartic, and non-minimal potentials, providing an extension to earlier research on dark Q-balls with an effective field theory approach.

We investigated a specific cyclic universe model based on an $AdS$ cavity, where our cosmos is represented as Truncated Anti-de Sitter (tAAdS). In this model, matter that appears in our cosmos actually originates from the "hologram" or boundary universe. We established the connection between the bulk and boundary universes using the holographic principle, and found that the matter in the boundary universe consists of cyclic modes. Due to the accumulation of these modes, we were able to derive the rate of entropy production in both universes. Interestingly, the entropy generates hot plasma in both the bulk and boundary universes at the beginning of each cycle's "big bang", allowing for the conversion of this plasma into matter in subsequent cycles, a process known as reheating. As a consequence, we examined the relationship between the matter density in the universe and its initial conditions in previous cycles, and discovered a critical point where the current and future cosmic evolution may be determined solely by a portion of the previous cycle's initial conditions. In this regard, we established an upper limit on the matter density in the universe, which corresponds to the upper limit on the dark energy scale, and may be related to the hierarchy problem.

Given a graph G, let's denote its vertex set by V(G) and edge set by E(G). A Hermitian matrix can be associated with this graph, and we can obtain the scattering matrix concerning this Hermitian matrix based on a large scalar parameter t. This study expresses the (i,j)-th element of the scattering matrix H(t) in terms of the number of directed Hermitian walks of length 2t on an ordinary graph G that start and end at vertices i and j, respectively. A key finding resulting from this expression is a new spectral criterion for determining whether the adjacency matrix of a graph G is non-singular.

We derive new conclusions regarding the Leopoldt property for certain non-commutative extension structures, particularly those related to Iwasawa theory. This involves establishing new proof for a previously demonstrated connection between commutative and non-commutative Iwasawa theory, as well as providing new insights into the nature of these theories. Our research also offers a simplified, purelly algebraic proof for a key result in non-commutative Iwasawa theory, and leads to important implications for the study of p-solvable groups.

We examine how accurately Belle II can measure displacement and how this compares to Belle II's ability to detect light-shining-through-a-wall experiments, specifically focusing on algebraic hidden particles from $B$ meson decays. We propose an experimental setup involving two vacuum chambers where an observer searches for hidden sector particles produced in one chamber and shone as light into the other, providing an alternative to measuring the displacement of such particles, especially those emitted alongside neutrinos. Using Belle II's data sample, our analysis shows that the experiment can clearly distinguish between particles that seeably travel a certain distance and those that are invisible, assuming certain conditions about the involved masses and coupling strengths, particularly when particles that seeably travel certain distances involve the emission of neutrinos.

The prevalence of online text data has prompted a detailed exploration of linguistic patterns, with contextualized language models enabling the extraction of hidden meanings. One of the most intriguing aspects for investigation is how language evolves over time, reflected in corpora that span multiple decades or even centuries. By analyzing multi-era datasets, researchers can examine semantic shifts and explore the complex dynamics of language changes. These analyses require advanced contextualized language frameworks capable of capturing both nuanced and historical semantics, as well as documenting the contextualized knowledge they encode. This paper provides a detailed exploration of current language frameworks in the context of semantic change studies, as well as future research directions in this evolving landscape.
